definition: A very large model trained on broad data at scale that can be adapted to many downstream tasks and domains.
details: The Stanford “foundation models” report coined the term to describe models trained on broad data with massive scale, whose emergent capabilities are then steered by fine-tuning, prompting or adapters. They function as a shared substrate that many applications build upon, raising both opportunities (few-shot learning, transfer) and risks (bias, misuse, environmental cost).

explainer.lead: A foundation model is a shared starting point for many AI applications, rather than a model built for just one job. Its broad training can enable useful new capabilities, but adapting and deploying it also requires care around bias, misuse and environmental cost.

tiers.eli5: Imagine learning a little about many subjects before choosing a school project. That broad learning gives you a head start, and a few hints or extra practice can help you tackle a particular project. A foundation model works similarly: it learns from lots of varied data, then people guide it toward different tasks.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers start with a large pre-trained model and steer it with fine-tuning, prompting or adapters for a downstream task. This can support few-shot learning and transfer without building a separate model from scratch for every application. Evaluation should account for inherited bias and misuse risks, while training and deployment choices should also consider environmental cost.
tiers.paperLevel: A foundation model is a model trained on broad data at massive scale and adaptable to many downstream tasks and domains. The term was coined in the Stanford “foundation models” report, which describes emergent capabilities steered through fine-tuning, prompting or adapters. Its shared substrate creates opportunities for few-shot learning and transfer, alongside risks including bias, misuse and environmental cost.

explainer.example: A model trained broadly can be prompted to perform a downstream task with only a few examples. The same model could instead be adapted with an adapter for a different domain, so both applications share one foundation rather than requiring two models trained from scratch.

usedIn.name: Few-shot learning
usedIn.detail: Applications can tackle tasks with only a small number of examples.

usedIn.name: Transfer learning
usedIn.detail: Capabilities learned from broad data can be carried into downstream tasks.

usedIn.name: Domain-specific applications
usedIn.detail: Fine-tuning, prompting or adapters can steer one shared model toward different domains.

explainer.intuition: Instead of training every AI system from the beginning, train one very large model broadly and reuse it as a common base. Different applications can then build on the capabilities that emerge from that training.
howItWorks: Train a very large model on broad data at massive scale.
Use the resulting capabilities, including emergent ones, as a shared substrate.
Steer the model toward a task through fine-tuning, prompting or adapters.
Build multiple downstream applications on the same underlying model.
Manage shared risks such as bias, misuse and environmental cost.
explainer.whyItMatters: Foundation models let many applications reuse broad capabilities, making few-shot learning and transfer possible. Because the same base is shared, its benefits and its problems can both spread into the systems built on it.
misconceptions: A foundation model is not limited to one downstream task; adaptability across tasks and domains is central to the idea.
Fine-tuning is not the only way to adapt one: prompting and adapters can also steer its behavior.
Broad training does not remove bias or misuse risks, and massive scale can bring environmental costs.
